Right after a storm, the watershed continues to put some base flow out and then it dries out and then it waits for the next storm. That's exactly what these case caddisflies will do, is they have the ability to weather the differential hydrology, if you will, because they can basically shut down and keep moisture in and then wait for the next moisture event. And typically in many, many towns, including your own, we look for opportunities for in kind mitigation, which means specifically restoration and enhancement and then creation if that opportunity exists. But usually the creation and the restoration components blend together because we don't want to take something that's already has an ecological value, whether it's upland or wetland, and take trees down to create a wetland just to create a wetland. So we always look for opportunities

to restore first. If you have a degraded wetland, we go after that. If there's a wetland that's not functioning particularly well, we can enhance it, we do that. And then creation is sort of the last thing that we do in that hierarchy after, of course, after the avoidance part.
